prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, enabling measurement of time and frequency at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: B014 is the strongest case once opening support is separated from merit and the record is checked for who did the original work. Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and first lattice-clock demonstration form the invention. Ye's group then brought it to the 1e-18 regime and used it for gravitational redshift tests and many-body clock physics. It is an invention that opens a door in the sense I care about: it lets us observe time dilation over centimetres, constrain drifting constants and search for dark matter. It has been reproduced and surpassed by independent laboratories, and it is the basis of the planned redefinition of the second. It carries a two-name credit with a clear division between concept and realisation, which is rare among the shortlisted entries. Seven of eight members place it in their top five, and I am treating that as corroboration of the reasoning, not as the reasoning itself.
statement.case_against: The honest reservation is overlap and category. Frequency combs (2005) and ion control (2012) were already recognised, so a sceptic can read lattice clocks as the next step in a prize lineage, an improvement in precision and not a new phenomenon. The redefinition of the second has not yet happened. There is also a priority question I cannot settle from the supplied record: whether Lemonde, Lisdat and other early strontium-clock groups, or the Ye group's Ludlow and Campbell, have claims that a two-name credit overrides. Separately, I ranked B042 first, and the committee should be wary of my own judgement there for the reasons stated in the conflict note.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B014 first and calls it a genuine conceptual step, not an incremental improvement: ultranarrow forbidden transitions with many atoms in the Lamb-Dicke regime, so quantum projection noise and Doppler and recoil shifts are controlled together. She also notes the allocation to Lemonde, Ludlow and others is not settled by the supplied credit.
responses.response: I agree and take the Lamb-Dicke argument as the strongest scientific statement of why the lattice clock is an invention and not a refinement of ion clocks. Where I want more care than she shows is priority. She is closest to this field, so I would ask her to check the 2001-2003 dates for the magic-wavelength proposal and for the first strontium demonstration against the historical record before we fix the citation. If Katori's priority holds, I accept her view that a two-person configuration is defensible despite the missing names.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B014 first as the clearest case of a measurement technique opening new observations, weighting coherence and linewidth control, and asks whether to wait for the formal SI redefinition of the second.
responses.response: On the redefinition I disagree with waiting. The Prize is for a discovery or invention that has been experimentally verified, not for a regulatory decision, and the verification is already in the agreement of independent clocks at 1e-18. A decision taken by metrology bodies is a consequence of the invention and not a condition of it. I do share his caution that the credit of other clock groups is not assessable from the supplied text, so the citation should name the invention and not a list of applications.

responses.point: Pearce ranks the IceCube entry B021 first as a detector-driven discovery that opened high-energy neutrino astronomy. He is candid that independent confirmation is still thin and that fair allocation among founders and construction leaders is unverified.
responses.response: I share the appeal of a new window. That is why I ranked B021 seventh and not lower. But his own caveats are the ones I weigh most: in a collaboration of hundreds, AMANDA and Baikal pioneers have claims, and the discovery is the flux and the technique, not yet a source picture. I cannot be absolutely sure we have identified the people who did the original work, and the supplied three names are disputed even among us, since I credited only two. I would keep B021 as a serious later candidate but not the prize this year unless the attribution record becomes clearer.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first as the natural continuation of the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits, a clean, widely reproduced discovery and the architecture for superconducting processors. He discloses his own proximity through WACQT and Chalmers.
responses.response: I appreciate the disclosure and share the closeness, since we are both at Chalmers. My difficulty is timing and distinctness, not quality. Circuit QED is later engineering built on the circuit quantum coherence that the 2025 prize recognised, and the boundary between the strong-coupling demonstration and quantum-computing engineering is blurred. Four other members put it low or off their lists, so it does not yet have the support that B014 has across the committee. I would not rule it out in a later year, once the committee has seen how the 2025 award settles.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks topological insulators B016 first as a new class of quantum states and notes the HgTe proposal credit (Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang) and 3D topological insulators fall outside the credited names, and that the prize scope would need careful definition.
responses.response: The science is strong and the theory-plus-experiment structure is what I value, with Molenkamp's HgTe observation as the original experiment. But as he says, the credit set is not clean: the HgTe prediction and the 3D work are outside the three names, and Zhang has died. Four of us also note the overlap with the 2016 prize. I would not choose a configuration in which we cannot name the people who did the original work with confidence, and that is the main reason I place B016 below B014 and outside my alternatives.

uncertainties: Priority among Katori, Lemonde, Lisdat and the Ye group's early strontium-clock contributors, and the exact dates of the magic-wavelength proposal versus first demonstration, needs checking against the historical record.
Whether the committee will regard the lattice clock as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.
Whether B042 deserves a prize without the STEM-corrector originators such as Krivanek, who are outside the credited names, and whether physics or chemistry is the natural home.
Whether B017 is early given the unsettled pairing mechanism, or is mature enough to be a next-year prize.
statement.conflict_note: Specific field connection: B042 (aberration-corrected electron optics) is in my own field of transmission electron microscopy at Chalmers, and I ranked it first. I would recuse myself from the final decision on B042 or at least ask colleagues to test my judgement for parochialism. Also, Göran Johansson (B009) is a Chalmers colleague; no personal tie to him affects my view. From my profile, no specific conflict is apparent for B014, B017, B016, B021, B008, B018, B020 or B001.
